item.content:encoded:
In the ongoing battle over a renovation of the Kennedy Center in Washington, DC,  the administration of US president Donald Trump has said it may have to demolish the Edward Durrell Stone-designed building and replace it with an amphitheatre.

This week, a Justice Department attorney filed a civil action stating the administration may seek to demolish the John F Kennedy Centre for the Performing Arts in Washington, DC, if renovations proposed earlier this year remain blocked by the courts.

The document cites the centre's lack of financial revenue and its decaying structure as the reason for renovation, stating the institution has lost "tens of millions of dollars each and every year" and that it is in a "financial and structural death spiral".

It proposed an outdoor amphitheatre in its place if the efforts to renovate and rename the building are blocked.

"Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheatre overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years," said the court filing.

"The Board recognises that President Trump's efforts and prestige provide the sole hope for the Center's financial survival, and structural renewal," the document continued.

"The Board also underscores, and the undisputed evidence demonstrates, that without the prominent recognition of The Trump Administration, and President Trump's efforts, the donors will not contribute, and the Center will continue to be in a financial and structural death spiral."

The building was designed by American architect Edward Durell Stone in the 19710s and serves as a major cultural institution in the city. It was established and named through a governmental statute.

It has been an object of debate since Trump replaced board members with his own selections in 2025 and had his name applied to the exterior.

Since then, his name has been applied to the building and removed by court order, and the administration has released renderings of its desired updates to the centre, which would require years of closures. These plans were blocked by the courts earlier this year.

Read:

AIA sues Donald Trump over Kennedy Center renovation in unprecedented coalition

This week, a judge will rule whether or not Trump can inscribe "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump" on the building underneath the Kennedy Center wordmark.

Earlier this year, a slew of donors and high-profile artists pulled out of supporting the centre and in the midst of its legal battles, visitors have significantly dwindled, according to The New York Times.

A coalition of architecture organisations, including the AIA and Docomomo US, also sued the administration over the proposed renovations earlier this year.

It is part of several building projects and proposals Trump has pursued for Washington DC, such as relining the Reflecting Pool in a bright blue and the "Arc de Trump".

item.content:encoded:
US studio Lehrer Architects has completed Loma Verde, a supportive housing development for once-homeless residents that features a slender footprint and stucco walls adorned with splashes of colour.

Located in the city's Filipinotown neighbourhood, the Loma Verde project was built on a tight lot that formerly held a single-family home.

At 4,500 square feet (418 square metres), the lot is about half the size of the average single-family lot in Los Angeles, according to Lehrer Architects.

"The site was extremely narrow and sloped in several directions," the team said.

For the compact site, the architects conceived a vertical, wood-framed building with 19 studio apartments for formerly homeless residents, along with offices for case managers. The site also features bicycle parking and a roof garden with expansive views.

"The architects designed a very thin, six-storey building with not an inch to spare," the team said.

"The vertical layering accommodates the units and the circulation, and spatially celebrates and separates them, adding to the building's delicacy in the landscape."

While technically a "single-loaded slab" building, Loma Verde has design features that give it a more dynamic appearance than a typical apartment block, such as bends and folds in the exterior walls.

The "visual excitement" is further enhanced by the exterior colouring – bright white intermixed with splashes of colour, such as lemon yellow and turquoise blue.

"The use of colour serves to celebrate all of the different architectural parts – from doors, walls and ground planes, to rooftop planters and even the exposed exit staircase," the team said.

Open-air corridors provide access to the living units, which range from 270 to 300 square feet (25 to 27.8 square metres).

One wall is lined with a kitchen and extended counter, which can be used for dining, working and storage. The units also have a sleeping area and an enclosed bathroom.

Natural air and light flow in through several windows, including a floor-to-ceiling sidelight next to the front door.

"Creating units that honour and nurture the tenants with a sense of generosity and joy was critical," said Michael Lehrer, founder and principal of Lehrer Architects.

The building has open breezeways meant to foster socialising and a sense of community, along with ushering in fresh air. The rooftop features colourful planters and views of the city, including the famed Hollywood sign.

The project's overall design was influenced by the work of several artists.

"Early inspirations for the design came from the color and light of California painter Wayne Thiebaud, combined with the compositional sensibilities of Richard Diebenkorn and the spatial sensibilities of Frank Stella's 2.7 dimensional paintings," the team said.

"These artists create worlds of visual impact within long, thin spaces on their canvases."

Read:

OMA completes first US affordable housing development in San Francisco

Loma Verde is meant to encourage the inclusion of affordable housing in Los Angeles, a city where the homeless population has climbed to over 45,000, according to a recent count.

"This project is a model of how a complete community should include multiple forms of housing existing in harmony together and caring for every resident, especially the most vulnerable," said Lehrer Architects.

"It also provides a blueprint for creative development in a city that urgently needs to increase affordable housing density."

Lehrer Architects has been "committed to creating ennobling shelter for Los Angeles's most vulnerable residents" for several decades, the studio said.

Its other projects include Willowbrook Apartments, which features living and community spaces for disabled veterans, and a village of brightly painted tiny houses that serve as temporary housing for homeless residents.

The photography is by Paul Vu.

item.content:encoded:
Skylights, an internal light well and silver-painted ceilings pull light deep into House in Shichiku, a home in Kyoto designed by local studio Tato Architects.

Designed for a couple and their cat, the home occupies an overlooked plot at the end of a small alley, on a site once occupied by the client's childhood home.

Responding to both the site's exposure and an existing mature tree, Tato Architects created a simple, metal-clad gabled form.

The studio rotated the house in plan, to create four different wedge-shaped gardens at its edges.

"The client's childhood home once stood here, and we wanted to keep as much of the existing garden as possible," Tato Architects founder Yo Shimada told Dezeen.

"By not facing the neighbouring houses head-on, four wedge-shaped margins appear at the corners, and each becomes a garden with a different character."

Contrasting the rotated exterior of House in Shichiku, its interior walls were aligned to the surrounding grid, creating an angular, kitchen, living space and study around a central dining area.

The home's dining table sits beneath a rectilinear cut-out topped by a raised table above, creating a lantern-like opening that allows daylight through the home.

Externally, the base of the home is wrapped by full-height windows that overlook the surrounding gardens, while the upper level was clad in sheets of corrugated metal.

The ground floor ceilings, which are just over two metres high, were finished with a subtly reflective silver paint, and the staircase can be closed by a wooden door to control how far the owners' cat can roam.

Read:

Kenta Hirayama clads House in Kinuta in steel-sheet facade

"At the centre of the plan we carved a void shaped like a miniature of the site outline, giving vertical release to the low, continuous space," Shimada told Dezeen.

"The reflective silver ceiling amplifies the ambiguity between the two geometries - the interior walls aligned with the city and the exterior walls that deviate from it - so that the way you perceive the space wavers," he continued.

"What began as a practical decision about height becomes the phenomenon that holds the whole house together."

The first floor bedrooms were organised around a central hall, divided by walls that stop short of the home's high, white-painted gable ceilings, allowing light from a series of skylights deep into the plan.

The grey plasterwork of the ground floor was swapped on the upper floor for a "wooden world" wrapped entirely in lauan plywood, which was also used to create desks, shelving and cupboards.

Other homes in Japan recently featured on Dezeen include the renovation of a 1970s home in Hayama by HYAN, and a blocky, wood-lined home near Tokyo by HYG Architects.

The photography is courtesy of Tato Architects.

item.content:encoded:
Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, known for her colourful polka dot artworks, has passed away in Tokyo from multiple organ failure at the age of 97.

In a statement, Kusama's gallery, David Zwirner, announced that she died at a Tokyo hospital on 14 August.

Born in Matsumoto, Japan, in 1929, Kusama was one of the best-known Japanese artists working today. After holding solo shows in Japan in the 1950s, her work evolved in New York in the 1960s, where she created performance art pieces and took part in exhibitions.

In 1989, Kusama held solo shows at the Center for International Contemporary Arts, New York, and the Museum of Modern Art, Oxford.

Kusama represented Japan at the 45th Venice Biennale in 1993 and her museum shows have drawn record crowds since the late 1990s, with a survey in 2014 based on museum attendance naming her the world's most popular artist.

In 2016, she made TIME Magazine's list of the 100 Most Influential People.

The artist became famous for her colourful polka dot paintings and sculptures, which include a gigantic polka dot pumpkin that is installed on a pier on Naoshima Island, Japan.

She is also known for her Infinity Mirror Rooms, immersive artworks in which the visitors step inside rooms that are lined with mirrors and lit to create a feeling of infinite space.

These have become immensely popular in the age of Instagram, with visitors often queuing to see them.

Read:

Yayoi Kusama installs mirrored orbs outside Liverpool Street Station in London

Kusama has also frequently collaborated with brands, including luxury brand Louis Vuitton, which a few years ago overhauled its stores with her polka dots and created lifelike animatronics of her for its windows.

Her work often interacted with the built environment, including an installation in a hurricane-damaged train garage on New York's Rockaway peninsula that she filled with 1,500 mirrored balls.

While her shows travelled across the globe, the artist herself, who suffered from hallucinations throughout her life, had lived in a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo since checking into it in 1977.

In a statement, her studio, Yayoi Kusama Inc, said the artist continued working up until her death.

"Throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant-garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction, and poetry," the statement said.

"She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul."

In 2024, Kusama created her largest-ever permanent sculpture, Infinite Accumulation, a series of connected metallic spheres located by the Elizabeth Line entrance of London's Liverpool Street Station.

The main image is courtesy of Yayoi Kusama.

item.content:encoded:
Around 1,800 people have pulled the keep of the historic Hirosaki Castle two metres closer to its original location in Japan's Aomori prefecture, following restoration works.

Using an ancient Japanese building relocation technique known as hikiya, the 360-tonne structure was placed fully intact on rollers and pulled by volunteers.

The hand-pulled relocation brought the castle keep, originally built in 1810, just over two metres closer to the 17th-century Hirosaki Castle complex.

The three-storey structure was moved from its original location in 2015 to undergo repairs to an earthquake-damaged stone wall, which was fully restored in December 2024.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by いいかも！！弘前（弘前市公式） (@e_comeonhirosaki)


The tower keep is journeying back to its original location following restoration works

According to the Guardian, around 1,800 people took part in moving the castle keep last weekend, tugging 30-metre-long ropes in rotating groups of 80 people.

The voluntary hand-pulled journey will continue for the rest of the month, with approximately 4,100 people expected to move the tower a total of five metres.

Read:

Swedish city of Kiruna wheels entire 672-tonne-church intact to new location

The remaining 73 metres the tower needs to travel will be carried out by machinery, bringing the structure to its final resting place before the end of the year.

Hirosaki city first announced a call for volunteers to take part in the hikiya process in 2015 when the tower was being relocated for repairs, allowing the historic structure to be moved without dismantling it.

Last year, the Swedish city of Kiruna wheeled a 672-tonne church in its entirety to a new location to accommodate the expansion of the world's largest underground iron-ore mine.

Other historic restoration projects that have featured on Dezeen include an upgrade to the 13th-century Clifford's Tower in England and the revitalised 17th-century Ottoman Seddülbahir Fortress in Turkey, which features timber elements that outline how its stone ruins would have looked.

The photos are courtesy of Hirosaki City.

Dezeen Events Guide has launched its digital guide and interactive map for the 2026 edition of London Design Festival, which enters its 24th iteration.

The festival takes place from 12 to 20 September, returning with a programme of talks, parties, exhibitions, installations, product launches, open showrooms and pop-ups.

The events take place across 11 participating districts: Bankside Design District, Blackhorse Creates, Brompton Design District, Chelsea Design District, Dalston to Stokey Design District, EC1 Design District, Fleet St Quarter, Mayfair Design District, Park Royal Design District, Shoreditch Design Week and Soho Design District.

Navigate the festival with our map

This year's guide features a map to help you navigate the 11 participating London Design Festival 2026 districts.

 

You can still be listed in Dezeen's digital guide to London Design Festival

Get in touch with the Dezeen Events Guide team at eventsguide@dezeen.com to book your listing or to discuss a wider partnership with Dezeen.

There are three types of listings to choose from:

Standard listings cost £150 and include the event name, date and location details plus a website link. These listings will also feature up to 50 words of text about the event.

Enhanced listings cost £200 and include all of the above plus an image at the top of the listing's page and an image in the listing preview on the festival guide homepage. These listings will also feature up to 100 words of text about the event.

Featured listings cost £400 and include all elements of an enhanced listing plus a post on Dezeen's Threads channel, inclusion in the featured events carousel on the right-hand of the festival guide homepage for up to two weeks and 150 words of text about the event. This text can include commercial information such as ticket prices and offers, and can feature additional links to website pages such as ticket sales, newsletter signups, etc.

About Dezeen Events Guide

Dezeen Events Guide is our guide to the best architecture and design events taking place across the world each year.

The guide is updated weekly and includes virtual events, conferences, trade fairs, major exhibitions and design weeks.

For more details on inclusion in Dezeen Events Guide, including in our guide to London Design Festival, email eventsguide@dezeen.com.

item.content:encoded:
Design practice Studio Three Sixty has created a temporary sauna that is being used as a theatre during Edinburgh's Fringe festival for the performing arts.

Designed by Studio Three Sixty director Lucy Osborne, who is also co-creative director of Sauna Sessions Arts Club, the functioning sauna can seat up to 82 people for performances.

"Sauna Theatre is conceived as a new kind of cultural space – the UK's first purpose-built sauna arts centre and the UK's largest sauna," Osborne told Dezeen.

"It disrupts the familiar architecture of sauna with the tools of theatre: lighting, surround sound and performance focus."

Located within the rear courtyard of Summerhall Arts in central Edinburgh, the venue will be hosting shows throughout the Fringe festival.

The performances will be based on the idea of Aufguss – a wellness ritual led by a sauna master, along with dance-based "rave" sessions.

The theatre space was designed to evoke a traditional sauna with Ayous timber benches arranged in a horseshoe shape around three large sauna stoves.

"The ambition was for the room to feel suited to the focus required by a performance but still unmistakably like a sauna," said Osborne. "We wanted the room to feel warm, social and collective rather than formal."

"Materially, we hope the space feels gentle and calm, so the internal timber was a key part of the design," she continued. "We used Ayous for the sauna benches and interior surfaces because it is a dark wood with a soft and cool quality to touch. "

The sauna was conceived by Sauna Sessions Arts Club founders Osborne and James Grieve after they observed numerous similarities between theatres and saunas.

By combining the two, they believe they have created a space with "a heightened communal state that is immersive and even transformative".

Read:

Eight relaxing home saunas for an instant wellness retreat

"We are massive sauna fans, thanks in part to spending so much time working on various projects in Norway and Sweden," said Osborne. "And as we sat in various saunas together, we started noticing that saunas have a lot in common with theatres."

"Both saunas and theatres are communal spaces where strangers share an intense, live experience together in real time," she continued.

"In each place, there's a kind of unspoken agreement to be present, to put daily life on pause, and to enter into a shared understanding with other people around you – strangers and friends or family."

Osborne and Grieve wanted the venue to be more than a giant sauna, with theatre lighting integrated into the design to allow the space to be transformed for each performance.

"We're not just putting theatre in a hot room," said Osborne. "We're trying to create a new cultural space in which to experience art whilst feeling great."

"There are no windows and the space is blacked out and lit by theatre lights, so we have complete control over atmosphere, emotional tone and colour," she continued.

"Keeping the heat in is a technical challenge in some ways, but the architecture also has to create the right conditions for a living and organic space which is managed by our sauna masters, with an ebb and flow of heat, cool air, water and steam."

Adding lighting and sound to the hot and humid space was one of the key challenges to enable the space to function both as a sauna and a theatre.

"Conventional theatre equipment cannot simply be placed inside a sauna – many components would get too hot, or would not withstand the temperature and moisture levels," said Osborne.

"We had to find a hybrid solution, combining fixtures that could cope with the sauna environment with six overhead glass windows, allowing a lighting rig above the room to shine down into the space," she continued.

"That lets us bring theatrical control and atmosphere into the sauna without compromising desired heat and moisture levels during performance."

Externally, the sauna theatre, which was designed to be dismantled and moved from place to place, features bright signage and includes numerous social and support spaces.

Along with showers, changing rooms and lockers, there is also a cold plunge pool.

Overall Osborne and Grieve hope that the Sauna Theatre will introduce some people to sauna and demonstrate how theatre can be part of people's wellness routines.

"We know many of our audience members will be first-time sauna goers, and that is a thrilling responsibility," said Osborne.

"We have created Sauna Theatre in the fundamental belief that art and culture are good for human beings – and that 'wellness' shouldn't exclude things like reading, going to the theatre, or listening to music," she continued.

"Good theatre sends you back out into the world a different person from the one who arrived, and this is our hope for Sauna Theatre. That great artists can harness delicious heat to take us on magical journeys and leave us surprised, delighted and changed."

Recent saunas featured on Dezeen include a crystal-shaped sauna in Sweden and a floating timber sauna on a lake in rural Norway.

The photography is by Paul Zanre, unless stated.

item.content:encoded:
Boutique hotel brand Aethos has opened its first London outpost with interiors designed by Astet Studio in a Ron Arad Associates building that was formerly home to Nobu Hotel Shoreditch.

Created by Astet Studio, the interiors of Aethos London Shoreditch were designed to blend the industrial design language of the original building with a softer Japanese-inspired material palette.

"When we first approached the project, we saw an opportunity to explore what we call East meets East," Astet Studio co-founder Oscar Engroba told Dezeen.

"Rather than recreating Shoreditch's industrial past, we wanted to bring its existing character into conversation with the precision and craftsmanship of Japanese design traditions."

The Barcelona-based interiors studio was inspired by the Japanese concept of Utsuroi for the project, explaining to Dezeen that its employment meant "the architecture stays constant while the experience quietly evolves".

Astet Studio used the Japanese concept of Utsuroi to evolve the hotel's lobby, bar, gym, members' lounge and Mitsu restaurant.

The 164-room hotel, originally built in 2017, is defined by its striking industrial facade, featuring cantilevered balconies framed in glass, steel, and concrete.

Guests enter through this layered concrete facade into an open lobby  characterised by earthy browns and muted natural tones, which was designed to introduce warmth into the industrial setting.

"We wanted guests to feel welcome and connected to the rhythm of Shoreditch, while still offering moments of calm," said Engroba.

"The colour palette draws from the Japanese Shin-Bijutsukai movement, using natural materials, planting and filtered light to soften the architecture without diminishing its character."

Contemporary, low-height seating was used throughout the space, while a series of large, textured rugs zone the space to create areas of relaxation.

Vintage decorative pieces and furniture were used intentionally throughout the lobby alongside works by local artists and designers to connect the interior to its east London roots.

Astet Studio brings warmth and tactility to the industrial spaces by using bespoke wood panelling across the lobby area, breakfast rooms and bedrooms.

"The palette combines hand-finished timber, textured ceramics, woven fabrics and predominantly matte finishes," Engroba explained.

"By favouring materials that absorb rather than reflect light, the interiors develop subtle changes throughout the day, giving the spaces a quieter, more tactile quality."

In the bedrooms, the studio shifted the material palette to be simpler and more refined, featuring muted tones of grey, burnt orange, and blackened wood.

"In the bedrooms, the focus moves towards comfort, tactility and a quieter sensory experience," said Engroba. "Materials become softer, lighting more controlled and the overall atmosphere more intimate, creating a retreat within the city."

Other Japanese-style interiors recently featured on Dezeen include Mitsu restaurant in London and Genso restaurant by Joyce Wang Studio in Tokyo.

The photography is Pion Studio.

item.content:encoded:
Ecuadorian studio Caá Porá Arquitectura has worked with the local community to construct a pavilion in the Amazon rainforest that allows researchers to get a new perspective of the landscape in Pacto Sumaco, Ecuador.

Known as the WildSumaco Research Pavilion, the facility was commissioned by Francis Marion University to expand the American institution's research operations that have been going on for more than 20 years.

Caá Porá Arquitectura, which is based in Quito, was hired to create a laboratory and classroom that would be the first phase of a larger campus that could be a platform for research and education.

Completed in 2025, the facility allowed the university to launch intensive courses in which students will train alongside local families to be biologists and community park rangers from local naturalist guides.

"We imagined this laboratory as a place of learning that lives within the forest, where changing light through the canopy and the sounds of the surrounding habitat shape the experience of the building," design team members Gabriel Moyer-Perez and Paula Izurieta told Dezeen.

It was conceived as a workshop rather than a conventional construction site with multiple collaborations.

Community members helped the design team understand the forest and techniques for preparing materials, biologists provided the climate control strategies needed for the laboratories and the architects contributed the joinery systems and the use of space.

Each technician was paired with more than fifteen hired community assistants, who became teachers themselves over time.

Located at the foot of the Sumaco volcano where the Andean slope meets the high Amazon, the pavilion falls into one of Ecuador's most biodiverse territories, and the surrounding forest is more than just a backdrop.

"Building here demands listening before imposing, taking the context as a whole as a starting point rather than an obstacle," the studio said. "It is an architecture that touches the site with care, aware that every support modifies a much wider web of relationships than that of the building itself."

The two-level pavilion sits in a clearing and lifts off the forest floor, allowing the terrain to remain active, water to circulate and the vegetation to continue around the building.

Its lower level holds research and analysis spaces, while the upper level serves as a classroom and bird observatory with floor-to-ceiling glass and mesh enclosures fitted with bird-safe protection.

Read:

Al Borde Arquitectos uses adobe for "biosecure" laboratory in Ecuador

"As the second level rises to the canopy, the bird observatory reveals a new perspective on the forest, making the changing relationships between the understory and the treetops part of the learning experience," Moyer-Perez and Izurieta said.

Above, the pitched roof collects rainwater through an asymmetrical butterfly profile that echoes the irregularity of the forest.

Sourced from the region, the material palette comprises Guadua bamboo, structural timber, fibers and stone – selected for their technical, cultural and environmental value.

"All the soil used in the bahareque walls, combined with cabuya fiber and lime over the guadua cane, came from the same excavation carried out for the biodigester and the foundations, resulting in an envelope with a low environmental footprint and high thermal performance," the studio said.

The team left portions of the structural timber and woven bahareque exposed to let the construction of the building be a teaching tool.

"Raw, tactile materials are combined with laboratory-grade finishes to create a pavilion that brings students, researchers and the local community into close contact with the forest while preserving the integrity of its ecosystem," Moyer-Perez and Izurieta said.

Other recent pavilions that allow occupants to observe the surrounding landscape include a red waterside structure by Dum Dum Lab in Chile and an expandable polycarbonate greenhouse by Office for Roundtable and JXY Studio in China.

The photography is by JAG Studio and Gabriel Moyer-Perez.

Collaborators: Josue Fernandez, Andrea Rodriguez, Gen Moya

item.content:encoded:
US studio IA has combined Craftsman-style detailing and a minimalist technical look with the details of a historic building for AI company Notion in San Francisco, California.

IA designed the headquarters for Notion, an artificial intelligence (AI) company valued at $11 billion, through five floors of the 1907 Monadnock Building in downtown San Francisco.

According to IA, Notion originally came to them with a brief for a "clean and light" approach that didn't involve traditional detailing.

However, in its peeling back of remodels from past tenants, including Uber, IA discovered historic materials and details, shifting the goals of the design to accommodate the building's historic resource. This included Columbia Marble floors hidden under linoleum and wood sliding-sash windows.

The studio implemented the Craftsman style to bridge the gap, repairing the historical detailing in the process.

"As this project progressed and more of the historic building revealed itself, the concept shifted to intentionally honor the property's history while remaining true to the spirit of the original design aesthetic," IA design director Kristoffer Tendall told Dezeen.

"We proposed the Craftsman style to combine the two, using simple and timeless details with clean and square edges," he continued. "This maintained Notion's core aesthetic principles while acknowledging the building's roots."

The five floors of work and amenity spaces feature lounge areas, a training room and a library.

Entrance to the building is through an adjacent alleyway, and the lobby features a burled-wood reception desk and a prominent Gerrit Rietveld chair.

Throughout, the studio used custom-stained cherry wood for the wainscoting, decorative ceiling panels and on the wrap-around staircase that descends into the private cafe.

Its central lobby area features drapery that can be pulled to create private space between waist-height wood-clad dividers.

The curtains are echoed in one of the primary work halls, which feature cafeteria-style seating and break-out areas.

Read:

Charlap Hyman & Herrero adds custom workstations to futuristic LA office

IA's Craftsman references can be most seen in the library, which features a geometric decorative ceiling and a higher wainscoting profile with tiered capitals.

Throughout, rich tapestry rugs are paired with mid-century modern furniture, much of it wooden as well. The whole of the interior is oriented around a central courtyard, which was also updated for use by the company.

Tendall also said that the windows were oriented to take in views of the surrounding historic district as well as opening up the space to highlight the historic details.

"Little design moments were added to further honor the building's historic components, including a fire-rated window in the lounge that creates a featured view to the historic cast-bronze interior stair, and reclaimed bar tops found in basement storage that were repurposed standing bar rails," he said.

"Several prohibition-era objects found during construction were preserved and displayed, as well as a framed original section of the blueprint, helping to honor and tell the unique story of the building."

He added that the team subtly highlighted disjunctions between the historic layouts and the renovation.

"For example, when the existing marble floors didn't perfectly match the office's new layout, the remaining infill was intentionally completed in wood rather than a traditional marble patch, helping to subtly feature the building's prior history."

The offices are one of many build outs happening in the Bay area as AI companies need more space and reach higher funding thresholds.

Notion global head of real estate Michael McGinley said the office represents a shift in offices from individual-centric to more community oriented.

"Office spaces across San Francisco became playgrounds, instead of thoughtfully designed spaces like the office we have here at Notion," McGinley told Dezeen.

"At our offices, for instance, we designed our space for the company rather than the individual. That means no ping-pong tables, and instead an actual Tools and Crafts room, where employees can be physical tool makers, not just digital ones."

Other recent projects from San Francisco includes OMA's first fully affordable housing block in the US.

The photography is by Garret Rowland.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a gravity-powered mountain trike designed to extend mountain tourism beyond the ski season is among the projects from the University of Ljubljana.

Also featured is biodegradable play equipment made from urban leaf waste and a multisensory exhibition system designed to make artworks more accessible to blind and partially sighted visitors.

University of Ljubljana

Institution: University of Ljubljana
School: Academy of Fine Arts and Design
Course: Industrial Design (BA), Industrial Design (MA), Graphic Design (BA)
Tutors: Patrik Bevec, Boštjan Botas Kenda, Žan Brezec, Rok Kuhar, Tamara Lašič Jurković, Jure Miklavc, Barbara Predan, Tim Prezelj and Barbara Prinčič

School statement:

"At the University of Ljubljana's Academy of Fine Arts and Design, industrial design is taught as a critical, research-led practice for engaging with the social, technological and environmental conditions shaping contemporary life.

"Slovenia's only university-level industrial design programme offers a continuous path from BA and MA study into interdisciplinary doctoral research, bringing together design practice, theory, strategic thinking and material experimentation.

"Project-based teaching sits at the centre of the programme. Students work across disciplines and within an internationally connected network of academic, public and private partners, addressing real-world challenges through product and service design, circular strategies, social innovation and critical speculation.

"They develop ideas through research, prototyping and testing, supported by tutors whose expertise spans academic inquiry and professional practice.

"The programme is further distinguished by its research in design culture and visual literacy. This foundation enables students to question established assumptions, understand how design shapes behaviour and meaning, and communicate complex ideas with clarity.

"It also expands the field beyond conventional human-centred approaches to consider systems, environments and more-than-human perspectives.

"The projects presented here show this approach in action: from biodegradable materials and inclusive exhibition tools to shared mobility, speculative interfaces and new models for year-round tourism.

"Together, they demonstrate how rigorous research, experimental thinking and close engagement with context can produce design that is imaginative, responsible and relevant."

Leafo by Iva Ferlinc and Maja Selinšek

"Leafo transforms urban leaf waste into biodegradable tools for open-ended sand play.

"Developed as an alternative to plastic beach and playground toys, the project connects two overlooked urban conditions: the disappearance of sandpits from public playgrounds and the seasonal accumulation of fallen leaves, often burned as waste.

"Processed leaves are combined with natural binders and plant-based pigments to create tactile, nature-inspired forms that invite sensory exploration, imagination and experimentation.

"After use, the tools can be composted, returning to the soil to complete a regenerative material cycle."

Students: Iva Ferlinc and Maja Selinšek
Course: Industrial Design (MA)
Tutors: Tamara Lašič Jurković, Jure Miklavc, Barbara Predan, Tim Prezelj and Barbara Prinčič
Email: iva.ferlinc[at]outlook.com and maja.selinsek[at]gmail.com

Hella Atmospheric Lighting by Žan Brezec and Rok Kuhar

"Developed in collaboration with international automotive lighting specialist Hella, this project reimagines the parked car as a portable social hub.

"Extending atmospheric lighting beyond the vehicle interior, it combines a car-body lighting system with a responsive digital service.

"The physical system projects light into the surrounding environment, while the service generates visual scenarios based on location, mood and user preferences.

"Together, they allow drivers and passengers to transform campsites, viewpoints and other temporary gathering places into immersive, personalised settings.

"By treating the car as more than transport, the project explores how automotive lighting can shape shared experiences beyond the road."

Students: Žan Brezec and Rok Kuhar
Course: Industrial Design (MA)
Tutors: Žan Brezec, Rok Kuhar and Jure Miklavc

Multisensory Exhibition Experience by Zoja Čepin

"This multisensory exhibition system makes artworks accessible beyond sight by combining layered tactile booklets with audio description.

"Each booklet translates an artwork into three progressively detailed tactile layers, allowing visitors to move from composition to key features at their own pace.

"Developed through interviews and testing with blind and partially sighted people, the system is simple to produce, affordable and easy to integrate into displays without altering them.

"Museums and galleries can adapt it with communities for permanent or temporary exhibitions, while visitors may take the booklets home.

"The result is a richer, more inclusive encounter with art for everyone."

Student: Zoja Čepin
Course: Industrial Design (BA)
Tutor: Jure Miklavc
Email: zoja.cepin[at]gmail.com

Šerkul – a circular bike-sharing service for Ljubljana by Patrik Bevec

"Šerkul is a station-free bicycle-sharing service that turns Ljubljana's discarded bikes into a shared urban resource.

"Recovered bicycles are repaired in a community workshop – fitted with GPS trackers and 3D-printed locks – and added to a mobile platform where users can locate and select them by size.

"Rather than building docking infrastructure, the service operates through a network of cultural institutions, public organisations, cafes and shops.

"Cycling earns users "green points", redeemable for benefits such as library membership or partner services.

"By connecting repair, reuse, shared mobility and local rewards, Šerkul creates a circular system that keeps bicycles and value moving."

Student: Patrik Bevec
Course: Industrial Design (MA)
Tutor: Patrik Bevec

Sustainable Goat-Cheese Packaging for Kumparička Organic Farm by Lina Glavan, Ana Kovačič, Špela Novak and Vita Puc

"This concept for Kumparička Organic Farm in Istria turns goat's cheese into a sensory encounter with its origin.

"The pack pairs the cheese with herbs inspired by the Istrian landscape and a recipe for marinated goat's cheese, extending the experience beyond the product itself.

"A foldable structure brings together paper partly made from olive waste, biodegradable whey-based bioplastic, untreated jute and recycled cardboard.

"Rooted in the farm's visual identity, its Mediterranean character connects packaging with landscape, craft and food culture while reducing reliance on conventional packaging materials."

Students: Lina Glavan, Ana Kovačič, Špela Novak and Vita Puc
Course: Industrial Design (BA) and Graphic Design (BA)
Tutors: Boštjan Botas Kenda and Rok Kuhar
Email: lina.glavan[at]gmail.com, spela.novak01[at]gmail.com, pucvita[at]gmail.com and ana003.kovi[at]gmail.com

Carrot Reader by Pia Golob, Florian Janez Gutmann, Maja Selinšek and Jovana Mališić

"Developed within the subject History and Theory of Critical Design, Carrot Reader challenges anthropocentric design by casting a houseplant as a tarot reader.

"Instead of allowing users to choose the cards, the device uses data from a moisture sensor in the plant to generate a different combination for every question.

"Giving a non-human participant control over the outcome, the project reverses hierarchies between people, technology and nature.

"Designed as a speculative companion for the home or office, Carrot Reader proposes an unusual exchange: the plant receives water and care, while its human caretaker receives more-than-human guidance in return."

Students: Pia Golob, Florian Janez Gutmann, Maja Selinšek and Jovana Mališić
Course: Industrial Design (MA)
Tutors: Tamara Lašič Jurković and Barbara Predan
Email: piagolob01[at]gmail.com, gutmann.florian[at]gmail.com, maja.selinsek[at]gmail.com and jovanamalishic[at]gmail.com

Antidote – a gravity-powered mountain trike by Matic Čič and Vid Lebič

"Antidote is a gravity-powered mountain trike steered with the whole body through an innovative pendulum-based mechanism.

"By translating the rider's weight shifts into smooth, carving-like turns, it creates a downhill experience between sledding, skiing and mountain biking.

"Developed with input from ski-resort operators and refined through iterative testing, the project culminated in a fully functional prototype.

"Responding to snow-scarce winters, it enables lower-altitude resorts to extend their offering beyond the ski season by reusing existing slopes and lift infrastructure.

"With no onboard motor and minimal need for new construction, Antidote proposes a low-impact route towards year-round mountain tourism."

Students: Matic Čič and Vid Lebič
Course: Industrial Design (MA)
Tutors: Jure Miklavc and Barbara Predan
Email: Matic[at]cic.si and ebic.vid[at]gmail.com

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Pearce+ has added a wildlife tower for bats, owls, kestrels, invertebrates and wetland species at Honeygar Farm in Somerset, UK.

Built almost entirely from reclaimed materials found on the farm, the wildlife tower forms part of a wider plan to restore a wetland habitat on the Somerset Levels.

"The core idea was to create a long-term piece of wildlife infrastructure that could stand the test of time and provide opportunities for as many different species as possible," Pearce+ founding director Owen Pearce told Dezeen.

"It sits within the wider wetland restoration of Honeygar, where Somerset Wildlife Trust is transforming a former farm into restored wetland habitat alongside a new research and education centre."

The tower was designed to become a home for numerous species of animals, which determined its overall form.

"Rather than designing a house for one species, we've tried to create the conditions for lots of different wildlife to move in," said Pearce.

Read:

Invisible Studio & Pearce+ top domed woodworking pavilion with aluminium shingles

"Different species need to nest or roost at particular heights, so the overall height of the tower is partly dictated by the animals it is designed for," he continued.

"Barn owls, for example, naturally seek elevated, protected nesting places. The size of the upper structure is then determined by the dimensions of the different wildlife boxes housed inside it."

The tower was built on masonry piers made from reclaimed materials as the site regularly floods. Above this, the structure was made from reclaimed timber and corrugated metal.

"The idea of the site's restoration informed how we built the tower," said Pearce.

"We wanted to use as few new materials as possible, instead reclaiming materials that were already available on the farm and giving them a new purpose as habitat."

According to Pearce, the process of utilising reclaimed materials added a challenge to the construction process.

"The biggest challenge is the amount of work and uncertainty involved," he said. "Reuse sounds simple but you have to find the materials, dig them out, move them, clean them, assess them and then work out how they can actually be incorporated into the building."

"You can design with an idea of what materials are available, but until you start building there is always an element of the unknown," he continued.

Along with specific spaces for barn owls, kestrels and bats, Pearce hopes that the structure will also become home to a wider variety of wildlife.

"The tower is intended to work at lots of different scales," said Pearce. "Untreated timber can provide habitat for moths, spiders, woodlice and other invertebrates."

"The reclaimed masonry has cracks, textures and cavities that insects and small animals can inhabit, while openings within the piers could be used by amphibians or small mammals. Rubble and earth around the base creates a hibernaculum, a damp habitat that might suit newts, slow worms and other wetland species," he continued.

"We've provided the infrastructure, but ultimately wildlife will decide how to occupy it. In a way, the exciting part is that the building isn't finished when we leave – its inhabitants will complete it."

Previously, Pearce+ created a temporary sub-zero restaurant in Canada and a woodworking shelter at Westonbirt arboretum in Gloucestershire.

The photography is by Samuel Bray.

item.content:encoded:
Designers from IKEA and Xbox were paired up to create the products in this furniture collection, including a stool that looks and tilts like a giant thumbstick.

Unveiled today at the Gamescom fair in Cologne, the nine-piece YXSTABY range is Xbox's debut foray into gaming furniture, designed to blend easily into the home when it's out of action.

"We set out to make furniture people really want in their home, not furniture they accept because it is what you need to game," said IKEA product design developer Philip Dilé.

Each of the pieces in the collection was designed by a team made up of one IKEA designer and one Xbox designer, uniting their gaming and furniture design expertise.

The standout product is a stool modelled on the distinctive thumbsticks found on Xbox controllers.

"We were looking at which objects people actually have around them when they play, and the thumbstick kept looking like a small stool to us," IKEA designer David Wahl told Dezeen.

Adapted from original 3D models of the device, the stool features a curved base that allows it to tilt in all directions much like the real thumbstick, allowing users to lean into the action.

The seat even has the same grippy tessellated edges, now serving to hold the sitter rather than their thumbs in place.

"The challenge wasn't creating a giant thumbstick; the challenge was creating a great stool that still felt like a thumbstick," Xbox design director Elliot Hsu explained.

"We went back to the controller's original design files and spent a lot of time refining the proportions, texture, seating curve and stability. We wanted people to recognize it instantly while still feeling comfortable and functional in a living room."

Other pieces that play on some of Xbox's recognisable design elements include a shiny stainless-steel platter and a cushion in the company's signature shade of green, both shaped to look like the controller's sunken cross-shaped D-pad.

Clever storage is another theme that runs through the collection, often set on casters or equipped with handles so it can easily be moved around the home and turn any room into a game station.

Read:

IKEA unveils inflatable chair that "challenges traditional gaming design"

Most notably, there's IKEA's first go at creating a TV stand since a failed attempt in 2012.

Set on casters, it can be rolled wherever it is needed, while opting for a square over a tubular metal frame keeps it from looking too much like office furniture, explained IKEA designer Lukas Bazle.

"Our focus here was to make a TV stand that's really safe, sturdy and affordable, and that looks good in a lot of different homes," he said.

"Doing a product like that at IKEA is sometimes harder than you'd think. We test our furniture very intensely, and with a TV and castors involved, a lot of things can go wrong."

There's also a wooden toolbox for holding various gaming gear and paraphernalia, which doubles as a laptop stand, as well as a rolling side table with integrated charging stations and a lounge chair with hidden storage pockets below the seat.

Its bouncy, cantilevered design was conceived to support both active and leisurely play.

"I hadn't thought at all about people playing in different modes," Bazle said.

"You sit forward when the game needs your full attention, and then there are games you play to relax, where you're sunk into the chair, and it's a completely different way of sitting. The lounge chair had to handle both."

The pieces are rendered in timber and muted neutrals of black, white and grey, with splashes of green guiding the eye to the integrated storage.

IKEA has gone full-force on gaming furniture in recent years, with previous launches including an inflatable gaming chair and a range of high-tech desks and chairs with Republic of Gamers.

item.content:encoded:
Developer Riksbyggen and creative agency BBDO Nordics have designed three flats based on what a 25-year-old can afford to buy in Sweden today, with the smallest micro home measuring just 1.9 square metres.

The sizes of the three apartments were based on Riksbyggen's square metre index, which calculates how many square metres of housing a young person can afford based on income, property prices and mortgage conditions.

The calculations were made using data from government agency Statistics Sweden (SCB) and digital bank Avanza.

Riksbyggen and BBDO Nordics looked at incomes in three Swedish cities – Stockholm, Gothenburg and Umeå – to create a broad geographical spread when calculating the size of the homes, which the companies are calling Sweden's smallest apartments.

"Stockholm, Gothenburg and Umeå are among the Swedish cities where young people have a particularly strong need for housing, while also facing significant difficulties finding and affording it," BBDO Nordics art director Anton Bolin told Dezeen.

"Together, the three cities show that the issue affects young people across Sweden, from south to north."

After calculating what a 25-year-old with the national average income and savings could afford to buy in each city, the companies designed three tiny apartments: one measuring 1.9 square metres for Stockholm, a 3.1-square-metre flat for Gothenburg and a 4.5-square-metre home for Umeå.

"The idea is to make the housing crisis facing young people visible and tangible," Bolin said. "We see numbers and statistics about it everywhere, but they can easily become abstract."

"So we wanted to show exactly how much home an average 25-year-old can afford today, and let people experience that reality."

Bolin then worked with Bengt Svedlund from Stockholm company Dekormakarna to create the three flats, which were designed to look typically Swedish.

"We wanted the houses to look like typical Swedish homes, the kind of houses you see all over the country," Bolin said. "With familiar architecture and details, but at an unusual scale that makes the absurdity of the situation immediately clear."

Each of the three buildings has a distinctive design, ranging from more classical building types to contemporary housing.

"The first is inspired by turn-of-the-century style, with a rendered facade in 'Stockholm yellow', herringbone flooring, mullioned windows and ceiling mouldings," Bolin explained.

Read:

Eight innovative micro homes that make small sites feel big

"The second draws on 1930s/40s functionalism, with clean lines, light pastel colours, linoleum flooring and a corrugated metal balcony," he continued.

"The third represents contemporary housing, with a brick facade and simpler, more functional materials."

One in five young people in Sweden still live with their parents, according to Bolin, who hopes that the project will ultimately help to rally public support for more affordable housing.

"We hope the project gets more people talking about the problem and puts housing higher on the political agenda," he said.

"That's why we launched the project ahead of Sweden's general election in September 2026. Our hope is that the next government will take action on the three housing reforms we believe are needed."

Previous micro homes featured on Dezeen include a house in a former wind turbine and an "aspirational" housing prototype in India.

The photography is by Jörgen Brennicke from Rockson.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Colar has updated and extended a dilapidated adobe structure to create a single-storey home in Chiapas, Mexico.

Named Casa Estelí, the 162-square-metre dwelling combines the revived adobe structure with two new brick volumes, each sheltered beneath an expansive, self-supporting timber roof.

Colar centred the project around preserving the existing adobe structure, which involved securing its 30-centimetre-thick walls with vertical reinforcements and a continuous timber beam to ensure its seismic resilience.

To further extend its lifespan, the timber roof is structurally independent to avoid additional loads and complete with overhangs to protect the walls from erosion.

"The main challenge was adapting an existing adobe structure – whose original construction and structural behaviour were not fully known – to new uses without compromising its stability, particularly in relation to seismic demands," the studio told Dezeen.

"The independent timber roof then became a unifying element, connecting the original adobe structure with the two new brick volumes."

To complement the earthy tones of the adobe structure, the two new volumes were built using locally produced clay bricks with a wall thickness of 26 centimetres to match the existing structure.

The masonry was left exposed across the home's exterior and interior, where the use of brick is complemented by a pared-back material palette of exposed timber and clay flooring.

Read:

Al Borde Arquitectos uses adobe for "biosecure" laboratory in Ecuador

"We chose materials that could establish continuity with the existing adobe while remaining clearly distinguishable from it," Colar explained.

"The ochre tones and shared earth-based materiality create a connection between the adobe and brick, while the rat-trap bond provides insulation and a wall thickness close to that of the original construction."

At the home's front, the renewed adobe structure opens up from a spacious verandah to an open-plan living and dining area lit by clerestory openings.

Situated off the living area is the smaller of the two new brick volumes, which contains a study, bathroom and utility space.

Meanwhile, at the home's opposite end, an open-air corridor links to the larger extension, which accommodates the home's two bedrooms and a shared bathroom finished in glossy green tiles.

Elsewhere in Mexico, Studio Font has perched a cliffside home on a series of inhabitable concrete columns and L-shaped roofs top the four volumes that make up a house in Los Cabos.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: US technology company Dell has incorporated Nvidia GPUs and AI-assisted visualisation technologies into its workstation portfolio to support its latest real-time design studio.

According to Dell, advances in graphics processing unit (GPU) rendering and AI-assisted visualisation technologies are helping to close the gap between initial design concepts and final client-ready presentations.

The company noted that real-time workflows are changing the way design studios work, enabling teams to create photorealistic images and explore multiple options interactively.

It also allows studios to test ideas and design iterations as 3D models are updated.

Dell also suggested that "visualisation is becoming part of the design thinking itself". This marks a shift from it being a specialist output at the presentation stage to being a tool for concept development and decision-making during the design process.

"The role of the visualisation specialist has been democratised to the role of the actual designer," Dell AECO alliances and solutions director Ken Flannigan told Dezeen.

To support these workflows, the Dell Pro Max and Dell Pro Precision workstations are equipped with the latest Blackwell generation of Nvidia RTX PRO GPUs.

These professional GPUs combine traditional ray-tracing hardware (RT Cores) with AI-processing capabilities (Tensor Cores).

The Dell Pro Max and Dell Pro Precision workstations support Nvidia's Deep Learning Super Sampling (DLSS) – an AI-assisted technology using pre-trained models to upscale images rendered at a lower resolution, generate additional frames, and improve ray-traced image quality.

According to Flannigan, this represents a change from relying primarily on increasingly powerful hardware towards combining GPU performance with AI-assisted processing.

"Now it's not just power – it's power plus these pre-trained AI intelligent models that are allowing you to work faster," Flannigan said.

"It's not that the GPU got faster, but that the intelligence behind the GPU got better," he added.

Flannigan noted that these advances may also improve energy efficiency by reducing power consumption and heat generation.

By processing visualisations and AI workloads locally on workstations instead of cloud-based services, Dell also suggested that studios can benefit from quicker workflows while maintaining more control over their design data.

Dell argued that while cloud-based services are important for storage and collaboration, local compute can be more predictable in terms of operational costs, as well as for intellectual property protection and data governance requirements.

"Bringing it locally means that you're buying compute, not renting compute," added Flannigan.

He noted this can benefit architecture firms working with sensitive project information and client data, which cannot always be processed through centralised cloud services.

Looking to the future, Flannigan noted that local computing will become increasingly important as design firms begin training AI tools on their own data.

"If we're all training visualisation and design aesthetics on a centralised data source, everything in the future designed by AI will eventually look exactly the same," stated Flannigan.

"So it's really important for designers to own their AI-trained design aesthetic," he added.

item.content:encoded:
Miami voters have approved Denver-based real estate company Oak View Group's bid to take over management of the city's historic Miami Marine Stadium and restore the structure.

Built in 1963 and designed by Cuban architect Hilario Candela, the concrete modernist stadium was closed in 1992 following damage from Hurricane Andrew and has sat abandoned for decades as the city and residents debated its fate.

The City of Miami put forth a special election on 18 August as part of the city's primary race, which included a referendum on a management agreement with Global Spectrum LP, a subsidiary of Oak View Group.

The referendum proposes that the group would oversee the activation and events at Miami Marine Stadium and its surrounding site, including a nearby marina and the proposed Flex Park for the area, with plans to transform the structure "into a reimagined state-of-the-art venue".

In a sample ballot, the referendum also states a 40-year term lease, and that Global Spectrum would pay the city up to $10 million towards the restoration of "the historic Marine Stadium". According to BoatingIndustry, there would be no cost to taxpayers.

Local group Breakwater Hospitality Group is also part of the management deal.

More than 68 per cent of voters approved the referendum.

"We are elated that the Miami community advanced this important step forward in the restoration of one of Miami's most treasured landmarks," said Oak View Group president of venue management Greg O'Dell in a statement issued by the team. "Miami Marine Stadium is more than a venue; it's a symbol of Miami's vibrant history and future."

Read:

Eleven architecture preservation battles across the US

"Alongside our Miami-based partners, Breakwater Hospitality Group, we aim to support the city of Miami in honoring its legacy while creating a vibrant space that will serve generations to come, celebrate local culture, and drive economic growth across the region."

The stadium's restoration is one part of a larger $80 million initiative to modernise and redevelop parts of the surrounding Virginia Key, a spit of land that sits in Biscayne Bay south of Miami Beach.

According to advocacy group Bring Back Marine Stadium and Breakwater Hospitality Group, next steps include "a comprehensive study and visioning process for the renovated stadium" by Oak View Group, who are set to work closely with the City, preservation partners, the community, and Miami's creative and business leaders on the project.

Contract negotiations for the management of Flex Park will also begin.

The team says the project will be "one of the city's most ambitious cultural revitalisation projects in decades".

This is not the first time the city and public have sought to support the resurrection of Miami Marine Stadium.

In 2016, Heineken and the National Trust for Historic Preservation hosted a crowdfunding campaign aimed at raising money for its restoration and conservation group Docomomo listed the structure as one of the most under-threat buildings in the US in 2022.

The photography is by Rick Bravo

Dezeen School Shows: a light made from organic waste from traditional Chinese medicine is among the projects by students at Politecnico di Milano.

Also featured is a modular mycelium habitat for sparrows, and materials made from salmon bones, skin and scales sourced from Japanese restaurants.

Politecnico di Milano

Institution: Politecnico di Milano, Design Department – Poli.Design
Course: Materials Design for Transition
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Sofia Soledad Duarte Poblete, Chengjun Li, Ziqian Yu, Malu Luecking and Francesco Cianfano, with the support of the Madetrans research group

School statement:

"Materials Design for Transition (Madetrans) is a research group based at the Department of Design of Politecnico di Milano.

"Founded in 2015 around the DIY-materials approach and led by Valentina Rognoli, the group investigates materials design as a central design practice, positioning its work at the intersection of sustainability, ecology, biodesign and regeneration.

"Its activities are also supported by the Biodesign Lab (B.Lab), the first laboratory dedicated to biodesign within the department of design.

"Through materials-driven and material-centred approaches, Madetrans develops theoretical frameworks, educational methods and hands-on experiments that foster new cultures of materiality.

"The group encourages designers to move beyond exclusively human-centred perspectives towards more-than-human and multispecies approaches, recognising ecosystems, living organisms and their interdependencies as active participants in design processes.

"Its interdisciplinary team brings together industrial and product designers, design engineers and fashion-system specialists, contributing diverse perspectives on material intelligence and its role in sustainable and regenerative futures.

"This selection presents ten student projects developed across courses in materials-driven design and biodesign. Through experimentation, speculation and applied proposals, they embody Madetrans' vision of materials design for transition and highlight an emerging field rooted in interdisciplinary collaboration, ecological thinking, biodesign and nature-driven innovation for broader systemic impact."

Reclaym by Anastasia Prozorova, Ivanna Harulia, Giulia Fabro and Marta Figueiredo

"Reclaym transforms discarded brick waste into a versatile material that combines structural resilience with tactile and aesthetic expression.

"Reclaimed bricks are pulverised into fine powder and mixed with different binders and aggregates to explore new formulations, textures and sensory qualities.

"The resulting samples retain the strength and memory of the original material while appearing unexpectedly soft, light or fragile.

"By inviting touch and challenging visual assumptions, the project reframes construction waste as a medium for creativity rather than merely a sustainable substitute.

"Reclaym demonstrates how reclaimed brick can bridge functionality, material experience and artistic experimentation in contemporary design and architecture."

Students: Anastasia Prozorova, Ivanna Harulia, Giulia Fabro and Marta Figueiredo
Course: Towards Regenerative Materials Driven Futures: Biodesign and Nature-Inspired Solutions
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Sofia Soledad Duarte Poblete, Malu Luecking and Francesco Cianfano

Mycelli by Golab Aminialiabadi, Rocco Carraro, Brigitte Guarneri, Keren Karsa, Shyam KS and Elena Pellegrini

"Mycelli explores mycelium as a responsive living material and a temporary interface for urban regeneration.

"Developed through observation, experimentation and material-led decision-making, the project embraces growth, unpredictability and multispecies interaction rather than imposing predetermined forms.

"It proposes a modular mycelium habitat integrated into architectural facades to support declining Italian sparrow populations in Milan.

"Designed for a six-month lifespan, the structure provides nesting space before gradually decomposing, after which its fibrous material can be reused by birds.

"By combining thermal, acoustic and electromagnetic performance with ecological function, Mycelli reframes architecture as a temporary mediator within regenerative urban ecosystems and multispecies coexistence."

Students: Golab Aminialiabadi, Rocco Carraro, Brigitte Guarneri, Keren Karsa, Shyam KS and Elena Pellegrin
Course: Towards Regenerative Materials Driven Futures: Biodesign and Nature-Inspired Solutions
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Sofia Soledad Duarte Poblete, Malu Luecking and Francesco Cianfano

Whynut by Nicole Dalle Molle, Giulia Luppi, Selma Wittermann and Mrunal Deshpande

"This project investigates nutshell waste as a resource for circular material systems.

"Through material characterisation and iterative experimentation, different formulations and processing methods were tested to assess structural, tactile and aesthetic qualities.

"The resulting composite showed rigidity, texture and surface characteristics comparable to wood-based materials, suggesting applications as a decorative finish.

"Beyond material development, the project proposes a regenerative system linking food production, waste collection, processing and furniture restoration.

"Rather than creating new objects, it upcycles existing furniture by replacing worn components with nutshell-based surfaces, preserving embedded value while reducing virgin material use, extending product lifespans and minimising further waste."

Students: Nicole Dalle Molle, Giulia Luppi, Selma Wittermann and Mrunal Deshpande
Course: Materials x Transition in the Master of Design for Sustainability and Regeneration
Tutors: Sofia Soledad Duarte Poblete and Valentina Rognoli

Orma by Ines Ravagani, Gülsüm Koç, Carloalberto Dusi and Mete Sümeli

"Orma reimagines pine needles, an abundant by-product of agriculture and timber production, as a valuable material resource.

"Through a materials-driven design process combining experimentation, material characterisation, research and documentation, the team developed a biocomposite whose properties ranged from leather-like flexibility to rubber-like resilience.

"These qualities led to the design of a bio-based, biodegradable footwear outsole that addresses the microplastic pollution generated by conventional soles.

"Rather than leaving persistent traces, Orma is conceived to return safely to natural cycles after use.

"The project demonstrates how overlooked waste streams can inspire material innovation while connecting circularity, performance and responsible product design in practice."

Students: Ines Ravagani, Gülsüm Koç, Carloalberto Dusi and Mete Sümeli
Course: Materials x Transition in the Master of Design for Sustainability and Regeneration
Tutors: Sofia Soledad Duarte Poblete and Valentina Rognoli

Trice by Josephine Plaum, Juliette Desertot, Matilde Reviglio and Nicola Sbrudolini

"Trice transforms rice-production by-products, including husk, bran, starch, fibre and broken grains, into 100 per cent compostable biomaterials without external binders.

"By combining the structural strength of rice husk with the binding properties of bran, the project develops materials that can be produced locally across rice-growing regions worldwide.

"Its prototypes demonstrate versatility, from rigid packaging components such as boxes and edge protectors to flexible bioplastic films for sealing.

"By redirecting residues that are often burned or underused, Trice closes loops within the rice value chain, reduces pollution and creates economic value while allowing materials to return safely to soil."

Students: Josephine Plaum, Juliette Desertot, Matilde Reviglio and Nicola Sbrudolini
Course: Materials x Transition in the Master of Design for Sustainability and Regeneration
Tutors: Sofia Soledad Duarte Poblete and Valentina Rognoli

Scravita by Chuyue Zhang, Junshuo Cui, Keyan Wu, Mingsheng Li, Kevin Yang, Yifei Li, Yuwei Ma, Jinghui Zhou and Chencheng Liu

"Scravita transforms salmon bones, skin and scales collected from local Japanese restaurants into a family of regenerative materials and a final lighting application.

"Through cleaning, enzymatic treatment, grinding, gelatin extraction and thermal modification, the project explores the structural, translucent and fluorescent qualities of seafood by-products.

"Material experiments combine salmon bone powder, skin-derived gelatin and heat-treated scales with natural binders to achieve different levels of hardness, flexibility and transparency.

"The resulting Salmorph lamp integrates these materials into a softly glowing cube, where fluorescent scales animate the surface under light.

"Scravita reframes seafood waste as a resource for circular, sensory and materially expressive product design."

Students: Chuyue Zhang, Junshuo Cui, Keyan Wu, Mingsheng Li, Kevin Yang, Yifei Li, Yuwei Ma, Jinghui Zhou and Chencheng Liu
Course: Materials for Product Design and Innovation
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Zhang Yu, Chengjun Li and Ziqian Yu

LumiStudio by Hu Yi, JiahaoHuang, Yumeng Li, Jiaxin Guo, Yanting Gao, Hanyu Wang, Wanming Feng, Youyou Li, Xindi Yang and Wenjun Ma

"LumiStudio transforms discarded flower tea residues collected from teahouses, restaurants and tea-processing sources in Xi'an into a series of translucent decorative materials.

"Through controlled experiments, the team explored butterfly pea, chrysanthemum, rose and lavender waste, adjusting binders, heating methods, moulds and drying conditions to preserve their natural colours, fibres and textures.

"The final pendant lamp combines selected samples with cotton threads, acrylic elements and 3D-printed supports.

"Illuminated from within, the suspended material pieces reveal varied translucency, surface detail and colour, presenting flower tea waste as an expressive resource for circular product design."

Students: Hu Yi, JiahaoHuang, Yumeng Li, Jiaxin Guo, Yanting Gao, Hanyu Wang, Wanming Feng, Youyou Li, Xindi Yang and Wenjun Ma
Course: Materials for Product Design and Innovation
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Zhang Yu, Chengjun Li and Ziqian Yu

Reshelled by Tian Bingxin, Li Ziyu, Chen Xinyue, Li Hongxi, Chen Sixiao, Fan Mingyan, Zhang Baoqi, Tu Yurong, Yu Siyuan and Wang Chongwen

"Reshelled transforms discarded seafood shells collected in Weihai into mineral-based materials for lighting design.

"The team processed shells from different species into particles of varying sizes and combined them with multiple binders to tune their strength, surface texture, colour and translucency.

"Further experiments focused on isolating the iridescent nacreous layer inside abalone shells. Vinegar was used to gradually dissolve the outer shell, revealing a clean and highly reflective inner layer.

"By refining particle distribution, moulding methods and material formulations, the project produced durable, glossy and light-transmitting samples.

"Two lamp prototypes demonstrate how shell waste can replace conventional decorative panels while retaining its natural lustre and marine character."

Students: Tian Bingxin, Li Ziyu, Chen Xinyue, Li Hongxi, Chen Sixiao, Fan Mingyan, Zhang Baoqi, Tu Yurong, Yu Siyuan and Wang Chongwen
Course: Materials for Product Design and Innovation
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Zhang Yu, Chengjun Li and Ziqian Yu

Osteomangus by Chen Zhang, He Mengfu, Li Yushuo, Sun Langjun, Zhao Qiyue, Li Yiming, Ni Zhenran, Cao Zhanchang, Sheng Xia and Li Kaifen

"Osteomangus explores chicken bones and mango pits as complementary waste resources for experimental material development.

"Chicken bones collected from a food-processing company in Shandong were cleaned, oxidised, dried and ground into mineral-rich powder, while mango pits sourced from local fruit vendors in Xi'an were processed into natural fibres.

"The team combined these components with gelatin, agar, starch, sodium alginate, mineral fillers and plant fibres to produce a diverse material library.

"Thirteen documented recipes range from flexible, translucent sheets to foamed, leather-like and rigid composites.

"Presented as a material cookbook, Osteomangus provides reproducible formulations while demonstrating the aesthetic and functional potential of agricultural and food-processing residues."

Students: Chen Zhang, He Mengfu, Li Yushuo, Sun Langjun, Zhao Qiyue, Li Yiming, Ni Zhenran, Cao Zhanchang, Sheng Xia and Li Kaifen
Course: Materials for Product Design and Innovation
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Zhang Yu, Chengjun Li and Ziqian Yu

Farewell Flower Goddess by Zhaoyu Chen, Kangrui Chen, Xuming Zhu, Boyu Zhan, Huanxu An, Hanzhi Xu, Yanqiao Peng, Xuhan Zhu, Zi'ang Wang and Fang Shi

"Farewell Flower Goddess transforms organic waste from traditional Chinese medicine into translucent sheet materials for lighting design.

"The team collected herbal residues from a local traditional Chinese medicine hospital in Xi'an and investigated how these discarded materials could be recovered as a design resource.

"Through repeated formulation and casting experiments, they addressed brittleness, excessive thickness, poor ductility and curling by adding starch, controlling sheet thickness and testing different herbal mixtures.

"Poria produces a pale, fibrous surface that gently diffuses light, while goji berry creates a warm amber-red glow. The final hexagonal lantern demonstrates how locally sourced medical waste can support circular material development and sensory product design."

Students: Zhaoyu Chen, Kangrui Chen, Xuming Zhu, Boyu Zhan, Huanxu An, Hanzhi Xu, Yanqiao Peng, Xuhan Zhu, Zi'ang Wang and Fang Shi
Course: Materials for Product Design and Innovation
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Zhang Yu, Chengjun Li and Ziqian Yu

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio KFA plans to convert a 1970s brutalist office in Los Angeles into housing after its recent designation as a historic landmark, taking advantage of a recently adopted adaptive reuse ordinance.

KFA's plans include converting the stepped concrete building in the city's Sherman Oaks neighbourhood into 95 apartments and turning its former laboratory and printing space into amenities.

The 165,00-square-foot building was designed in the 1970s by AC Martin & Associates to serve as the corporate headquarters of growers' cooperative Sunkist Growers.

Owned and operated by local developer IMT Residential since 2013, the building has been empty since 2015, following Sunkist Growers' relocation.

Following the building becoming vacant, IMT Residential enlisted architecture studio Johnson Fain to restore the structure and update it for seismic resilience.

Johnson Fain also designed a masterplan for the site along with several new buildings on the 8.3-acre site, now known as Citrus Commons.

Recently the building achieved Historic-Cultural Monument status from the City of Los Angeles and the developer plans to utilise recent changes in the city's Adaptive Reuse Ordinance (ARO) to convert the Sunkist building into residential.

According to Los Angeles City Planning, the updated ordinance grants exemptions to certain zoning requirements and reviews and expands the applicable area beyond the city's downtown.

Read:

Logic transforms bland commercial office into "humble and collaborative" workspace

IMT Residential selected KFA to carry out the building's conversion partly due to the studio's role in forwarding Los Angeles' first ARO in 1999.

According to the developer, the conversion will take advantage of its high ceilings to create residential units that range from studios to three-bedroom apartments. Under current zoning, the minimum square footage of a new residence is 450 and IMT Residential cited the smallest for this project at 516 square feet.

On the podium floor, the design will keep the mezzanines, integrating them into the apartments.

"Through adaptive reuse, Citrus Commons demonstrates how reimagined historic buildings can serve future generations while preserving iconic architecture," said IMT Residential in a press release.

The developer plans to begin construction as soon as KFA's plans are approved by the city.

Other conversions of brutalist office buildings include Becker + Becker's conversion of a Marcel Breuer structure in Connecticut into Hotel Marcel and OFIS Arhitekti's conversion of brutalist printworks in Slovenia into offices.
